content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed comprehensive guidance on HIV testing services (HTS), incorporating all current recommendations relevant to HTS. To facilitate the development of these guidelines, the WHO established three distinct groups, each tasked with specific functions. These groups were carefully composed to ensure a diverse range of expertise, experience, and representation across geographical regions, genders, and communities. 1. WHO Guideline Steering Group (SG): This group was led by the WHO’s HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infections (HHS) Testing, Prevention, and Populations Unit, which also served as the secretariat. Members included WHO staff from various departments, such as Essential Medicines and Health Products, Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research, and the Global Tuberculosis Programme. Technical staff from all WHO regional offices, country offices, other United Nations (UN) agencies, and partner organizations also contributed. 2. Guideline Development Group (GDG): This group consisted of 25 members, selected to represent a balance of geographical regions, genders, and professional backgrounds, including academia, research, program implementation, policy, and community organizations. The GDG was responsible for formulating new WHO recommendations, considering implementation and service delivery aspects, and reviewing and approving the final guidelines. Members were selected through a rigorous process involving curriculum vitae (CV) reviews, declarations of interest, confidentiality agreements, and public consultation. 3. External Review Group (ERG): This group included 83 peer reviewers from academia, policy, research, program implementation, and community organizations, including key population networks. Members were selected to ensure geographical and gender balance. The ERG provided critical feedback on the guidelines to ensure their comprehensiveness and relevance. Key stakeholders, including ministries of health, laboratory services, researchers, implementing agencies, WHO offices, UN agencies, community networks, and people living with HIV (PLHIV), were engaged throughout the process to update and synthesize key messages in the guidelines. Declarations of interest were submitted by all GDG members, non-WHO staff, and external reviewers, and no conflicts of interest were identified that would preclude participation. The scope of the guidelines was defined by mapping existing guidance, including updates since the 2019 Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services and the 2016 Guidelines on HIV Self-Testing and Assisted Partner Notification. Through this process, three critical gaps requiring normative guidance were identified: 1. Expanded use of self-testing, particularly in facilities, within pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) programs, and for caregiver-assisted testing of children aged 18 months and older. 2. Broader use of network-based testing services for all populations. 3. General use of recency assays within routine HIV testing services. Opportunities to integrate additional WHO guidance were also highlighted, such as self-testing and self-care across disease areas, and network-based testing services. Systematic reviews and a modeling study were commissioned to address these gaps, adhering to the GRADE methodology to assess the effectiveness and certainty of evidence. Reviews also considered values, preferences, feasibility, resource use, and equity. The GDG developed five PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions to guide the formulation of recommendations. These questions addressed topics such as the use of HIV self-testing in clinical settings, PrEP initiation and continuation, and the use of recency assays in testing services. Evidence was assessed and reviewed by an independent methodologist and the GDG, SG, and WHO secretariat. Outcomes were ranked on a GRADE scale to determine their importance. During 2022–2023, WHO convened virtual meetings to review evidence and formulate new recommendations. The GDG reached consensus on four recommendations, covering self-testing, network-based testing, and recency testing. Strong recommendations were made in favor of self-testing and social network testing. For recency testing, a conditional recommendation against its programmatic use was made, with some members favoring a stronger recommendation against it. No recommendation was made on caregiver-assisted testing using self-test kits for children. The guidelines were revised based on feedback from the GDG, SG, and ERG, and plans for dissemination were developed. WHO will assist member states in adapting the guidelines to their national contexts and will monitor their uptake and implementation through the Global AIDS Monitoring (GAM) survey, policy reviews, and stakeholder dialogues. Updates to the guidance will be considered as new evidence emerges.
